Karl was the only lighthouse keeper in the region, and he didn't mind at all. It was a simple life. Each day he checked the lanterns, made sure the mechanism rotated without fail, and read every novel the lighthouse library had on its shelves. But on his way to check the lanterns, a familiar, faint glow appeared off in the distance. 

In the middle of the ocean, Karl could see it for miles. He had to be careful though, as the sea was a tricky beast. It could calm one moment and roar the next, lashing at the vessel to cause seasickness in its victims. 

The light, the one he had seen every night for over three months, came closer and closer. As it neared, he could see that there were multiple beams of light, bobbing up and down. These were not lanterns but whales. 

Their bioluminescence was stunning. Like a million stars in the night sky, the ocean was lit up with dancing waves of sparkling green. But the lighthouse was not for Karl. It was for the sea. A guide to safety. Karl would not be the one to survive.

There were no words from the whales, no warning that the lighthouse was on its way down. There was no call to help. No chance for rescue. Only the lights of the whale, and the lighthouse that didn't keep him safe after all.<|end_of_text|>

I'm a keeper of a lighthouse in Iceland. The sea before me is calm, dark as midnight, and yet it glows like fire. The whales, hundreds, maybe thousands of them, are swimming, bioluminescence spreading like ripples behind them. Their tails cut through the water, and I see a flash of green, the deep green of seaweed, and another flash, of a color I don't know. Their songs rise up from the water and are carried to the lighthouse, where I can hear every syllable. This is the time for me to write my book. My book about the whales. My book about how they have always known me, and I, them. My book about how it all began with a young boy and a whale song.

But not now. The light must be lit before the keeper's story can be written. The light and the song and the sea.<|end_of_text|>

He took one last pull of his cigarette and blew the smoke into the wind before he dropped it to the ground and ground it out beneath his hiking boot. He would not be able to get far if his foot slipped on the rocky terrain, but the thought of being found in that state was too embarrassing for him to risk. He would be caught in the very first week of his new job at the lighthouse, and that could not happen. He had to prove his worth, show them that he could handle this position.

He began to walk east, the direction of the lighthouse, keeping his eyes open for anything unusual. But in Iceland's endless darkness, it wasn't until he saw the glow that he realized something was out of place. He shielded his eyes and stood still, trying to catch a glimpse. A group of whales had breached from the water's depths and the moonlight sparkled against their skin. The light shimmered and sparked, as if the whales were covered in stars. The scene reminded Hannes of something he had seen on the cover of a travel magazine. Bioluminescent whales, a strange and magical phenomenon. 

He watched them swim away from the shore, their beautiful sparkling bodies disappearing beneath the waves. And though he longed to follow them, he knew he had to get back to his new home, for a different sort of magical adventure.<|end_of_text|>

The lighthouse is high, high above sea level. There are no other people for hundreds of miles. The moon is full. It's not as bright as you might think, though -- the light refracts and bounces off the water, scattering in a million different directions. So you can't see for miles and miles at night. 

It's the keeper's second night shift, and he's been scanning the waves for any hint of a whale. Bioluminescent whales are hard to find at the best of times. And, after all, this is his second night in this isolated place. Not many people know about this lighthouse. 

But then... he sees it. Out in the deep, dark waters. The whale glows like a constellation in the night sky. He stops, completely amazed. For a few moments, everything stops -- no more cold wind, no more creaking and groaning in the tower. There's just him and that beautiful whale. 

Eventually, though, he snaps back to reality and turns to the door, intent on making a quick trip outside before heading back in. But when he opens the door, he sees a man in a black raincoat, standing in front of him. The man says nothing but simply holds out his hand, and the keeper takes it and follows the stranger down the winding stairs, not knowing what to expect.<|end_of_text|>

The lighthouse keeper woke up, and went out on the balcony. It was midnight, and the stars were twinkling, but something was out of place.

Below the cliffs was the Arctic Ocean. He could see a bioluminescent glow, which was not normal for an area of sea where no life was found, not for days or months at a time.

Curious, he took out his telescope and looked down into the sea. At first, all he could see was darkness. Then, a whale! One whale, and then another, came out of the darkness, and lit up like a firework.

Then, suddenly, all at once, the bioluminescent glow dissipated. The ocean went dark again. The keeper went back to bed, confused and full of wonder.

The next day, he spoke to other sailors, and they all said they had seen the same thing. They had seen bioluminescent whales. All of them. And they did it at night. They did it when it was dark.

They told him that the bioluminescent glow had come at midnight, and not a moment sooner, and it had been timed for a reason. And the keeper knew exactly what that reason was.

But he wouldn’t tell anyone, and he would never forget what he had seen. He had seen bioluminescent whales, and it would always be a mystery. He would never understand it, and he would never tell anyone.<|end_of_text|>
